name: pwntools
one_line: Python library for writing exploits and talking to CTF programs
plain: `pwntools` is a Python library (import with `from pwn import *`) that makes binary-exploitation challenges less painful. It connects to a program locally or over the network, sends and receives data, packs numbers into bytes, and builds payloads.
It is not a command you run, so this page is a guide to the functions you use most. Write a small Python script, run it with python3 and iterate.
The pwn command-line helper (pwn cyclic, pwn checksec, pwn shellcraft) wraps some features for quick use in the shell.
when: Talk to a service on a remote CTF port.
Send a buffer overflow payload with the right padding.
Build a ROP chain or format-string payload.
Check which protections a binary has.

examples.title: Run a local program and talk to it
examples.cmd:
from pwn import *
p = process('./vuln')
p.sendline(b'hello')
print(p.recvline())
examples.explain: process starts the binary. sendline sends text plus a newline; recvline reads one line back. Use bytes (b'...').

examples.title: Connect to a remote challenge
examples.cmd:
from pwn import *
r = remote('10.10.10.5', 9001)
r.recvuntil(b'name: ')
r.sendline(b'Alice')
r.interactive()
examples.explain: remote connects over TCP. recvuntil waits for a prompt. interactive() hands the keyboard to you, to use a shell you obtained.

examples.title: Find the offset with a cyclic pattern
examples.cmd:
from pwn import *
print(cyclic(200))
# crash the program, read the value in the instruction pointer, say 0x6161616c
print(cyclic_find(0x6161616c))
examples.explain: cyclic makes a pattern with no repeats. After a crash, cyclic_find turns the value found in the instruction pointer into the exact offset.

examples.title: Pack an address
examples.cmd:
from pwn import *
payload = b'A' * 72 + p64(0x401196)
examples.explain: p64 makes a 64-bit little-endian address; p32 for 32-bit. The padding fills the buffer up to the saved return address.

examples.title: Set context for the target
examples.cmd:
from pwn import *
context.binary = ELF('./vuln')
context.log_level = 'debug'
examples.explain: context tells pwntools the architecture, so packing and shellcode match. log_level debug prints every byte sent and received.

examples.title: Read symbols from a binary
examples.cmd:
from pwn import *
elf = ELF('./vuln')
print(hex(elf.symbols['win']))
print(hex(elf.got['puts']))
examples.explain: ELF gives function addresses (symbols), GOT and PLT entries and section addresses, useful for ret2win and ret2plt.

examples.title: Shellcode
examples.cmd:
from pwn import *
context.arch = 'amd64'
sc = asm(shellcraft.sh())
print(len(sc))
examples.explain: shellcraft creates assembly for common tasks; asm assembles it to bytes.

examples.title: Debug with gdb
examples.cmd:
from pwn import *
p = gdb.debug('./vuln', 'break main\ncontinue')
examples.explain: Starts the binary under gdb with commands. Needs a terminal such as tmux (context.terminal = ['tmux','splitw','-h']).

examples.title: Check protections from the shell
examples.explain: Shows RELRO, stack canary, NX and PIE. This tells you which exploitation techniques are possible.

mistakes: Sending str instead of bytes in Python 3: always b'...'.
Wrong architecture in context: addresses pack to the wrong width.
Forgetting a newline: sendline adds it, send does not.
Off-by-one in the offset: always confirm with cyclic_find after a real crash.
Testing with ASLR off locally and forgetting it is on remotely.
